headline: Markets eye a rebound as rate-hike talk builds before the RBI meet

segments.title: The big picture
segments.script:
Good morning. It's Wednesday, the twenty-fifth of November, and here are the three things that matter most today.

First, markets look set to bounce back. After Monday's steepest one-day fall in more than four months, GIFT Nifty is pointing to a gap-up open, helped by foreign buying and softer oil prices.

Second, the interest rate debate is heating up. The Reserve Bank's policy committee meets from the second to the fourth of December. S and P Global now expects a rate hike in December, while SBI's economists have scaled back their call to a quarter-point increase rather than half a point.

And third, the economy is running hot. Core sector growth hit a thirty-one-month high in October, factory activity is at a nine-month high, and several trackers call October the strongest month in years. But inflation pressure is building right alongside it.

segments.title: How markets closed
segments.script:
Now to how markets closed. Monday was a rough day. The Sensex fell 1.77 percent and the Nifty 1.75 percent, their steepest daily declines in months, with the Nifty ending at 25,349. Profit-booking hit banks, financials and metals hardest, and Bank Nifty tumbled more than 4 percent.

But keep it in context. Even after that fall, the Sensex is up nearly 11 percent this month, adding about 34.6 lakh crore rupees to investor wealth. Foreign institutional investors have been the big driver. Their net buying in November has crossed 1.27 lakh crore rupees, the highest monthly inflow on record, after they pulled out around 35,000 crore rupees in each of September and October. Domestic institutions, meanwhile, held an all-time-high 19.31 percent share of listed companies at the end of September.

This morning, GIFT Nifty futures were near 25,738, pointing to a strong start even though Asian markets are lower. One risk to watch, flagged by experts speaking to Mint: if the global AI rally revives, foreign investors who have been moving money into India since late October could slow down.

Now the levels. Analysts quoted by Moneycontrol see resistance at 25,500, and then 25,800 to 26,000. Dharmesh Bhatt of Systematix calls 25,700 the immediate hurdle. On the downside, the 25,300 to 25,200 zone is seen as immediate support, with 25,000 described as crucial.

segments.title: IPOs and deals
segments.script:
Now to IPOs and deals. Mahanadi Coalfields' IPO allotment is due today. Refunds and demat credits follow tomorrow, and the listing is planned for Friday, the twenty-seventh. NLC India Renewables is also in the pipeline. Mint points to its 16,204 megawatt renewable project pipeline and its Navratna parent, but flags high customer concentration and dependence on a few regions as risks. And the government plans to list IIFCL, the state-owned infrastructure lender, likely before the end of this financial year, through a mix of a stake sale and fresh shares.

In deals, Goldman Sachs and Societe Generale together bought about 1 percent of Lenskart for 920 crore rupees, at 725 rupees a share, from Steadview Capital. Lenskart shares still slid about 4 percent, to close near 716 rupees. The Reserve Bank has cleared SBI Mutual Fund to buy up to 9.99 percent of South Indian Bank, whose shares are at record highs. Tata Steel's two-part deal with APL Apollo Tubes will eventually triple its downstream capacity, but Mint notes both stocks slid on Monday as shareholders face a wait of three to three and a half years before earnings benefit.

Zooming out, private equity and venture capital investment in India hit 8.7 billion dollars in October. That's the highest monthly figure in five years, according to EY and the Indian Venture and Alternate Capital Association, with financial services taking 5.9 billion of it.

segments.title: Economy and policy
segments.script:
Now to the economy, where the October numbers keep coming in strong. Core sector growth hit a thirty-one-month high of 10.9 percent. Coal output rose 23 percent and electricity generation nearly 22 percent, though both were coming off a weak base a year ago. ICRA puts economic activity growth at a thirty-six-month high of 12.8 percent, and Jefferies calls it a four-year high of 9 percent. For November, the HSBC flash composite index edged up to 56.3, with manufacturing at a nine-month high even as services slowed. The big number, GDP, is due on the thirtieth.

The catch is inflation. Jefferies says price pressures intensified, and rural demand stayed weak after a subdued monsoon. Protein inflation is rising too. Milk, eggs, meat, fish and pulses are costlier, on higher feed and fodder costs, low rainfall, and maize being diverted to ethanol. And India's oil and gas import bill jumped 60 percent in October. The Indian crude basket averaged around 120 dollars a barrel, against about 65 a year earlier, and cooking gas use fell.

That's why the rate debate matters. S and P Global expects the Reserve Bank to hike in December and again in early 2027. It kept this year's growth forecast at 7 percent and cut next year's to 7 percent. SBI's economists now expect a quarter-point hike, warning that a jumbo half-point move could raise financial stability concerns and hurt growth.

On trade, India and the European Union are likely to sign their long-awaited free trade agreement on the sixteenth of December, after concluding talks in January. And an official says India and Canada are very close to finishing negotiations on their economic partnership pact, with a target of 50 billion dollars of trade by 2030.

With the Budget about two months away, the wish lists are arriving. The Confederation of Indian Industry wants the foreign investment cap in public sector banks raised to 49 percent. Aluminium product makers want customs duty on primary aluminium cut from 7.5 percent to zero. And Food Processing Minister Chirag Paswan says the 40 percent GST on low-priced beverages is a concern he will push to ease. One more: pension funds are tilting toward government bonds as their equity holdings near the cap, with UTI Pension Fund now putting half of its new money into government securities.

segments.title: Around the world
segments.script:
Around the world, the AI trade swung hard again. On Monday, the Nasdaq 100 surged almost 7 percent on news that Jensen Huang is returning to lead Nvidia. On Tuesday it gave back about 2 percent, as Nvidia shares fell sharply, by somewhere between 5 and 9 percent depending on the report, and investors braced for possible new US tariffs. The S and P 500 slipped half a percent, while the Dow rose nearly 1 percent to just above 50,000. Anthropic's shares dropped below their 83 dollar IPO price in only their fourth day of trading, and Hewlett Packard Enterprise fell 16 percent despite beating estimates.

In Asia this morning, the regional index is down about 1 percent after its biggest rally since July, and Korea's Kospi is reported down around 5 percent after a 6 percent jump the day before. China, meanwhile, is cutting the margin requirement for buying shares with borrowed money to 80 percent, from the thirtieth of November, to support its market.

On oil, Brent is just under 91 dollars a barrel, slightly lower, as worries about a supply glut offset attacks on shipping near the Strait of Hormuz. Not everyone expects that to last. Mirae Asset Sharekhan says the correction has gone too far and a sharp rebound is likely. And India and China are on track for record Russian oil imports this year, averaging 3.4 million barrels a day through mid-November.

segments.title: Your money
segments.script:
Now to your money. The Reserve Bank has proposed new digital payment safeguards. Under the draft rules, you could switch off UPI and other payment channels, set your own transaction and daily limits, and turn debit and credit cards on or off. Separately, the Reserve Bank has kept SBI, HDFC Bank and ICICI Bank on its list of systemically important banks, which means they must hold extra capital.

Two tax rulings worth knowing. The Delhi bench of the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal has sent back a case where a woman deposited about 58 lakh rupees in cash, which she said came from money her husband withdrew after selling agricultural land. The lesson is simple: keep the paper trail for large family transfers. In another Delhi tribunal ruling, a GST refund was held not to be automatically taxable just because it shows up in the tax audit report, where the GST paid had never been claimed as an expense.

For homebuyers, the Supreme Court has told courts to check whether banks followed construction-linked disbursement terms before chasing EMIs from buyers stuck with unfinished flats, which gives interim protection from coercive recovery. On retirement savings, the EPFO has proposed letting members put voluntary money straight into their UAN-linked accounts, without going through the employer. And new ESIC regulations took effect on the twenty-first, so sickness and maternity benefits no longer need separate claims.

Gold is under pressure. It fell more than 2 percent this morning as bets on rate hikes rose, wiping out most of Monday's rebound. Augmont's Renisha Chainani had said gains toward 3,700 dollars an ounce were possible if support at 3,500 held.

Two dates for your calendar. Central government pensioners must submit their annual life certificate by the thirtieth of November. And banks in Bengaluru are shut this Friday, the twenty-seventh. One warning, too: fraudsters are posing as SEBI-registered intermediaries to pull people into fake trading platforms. Verify who you are dealing with, steer clear of assured-return schemes, and report cyber fraud on the 1930 helpline.

That's the brief. Today, watch whether the opening bounce holds above 25,500 to 25,700 on the Nifty, and whether foreign buying continues after Monday's sell-off. Check your Mahanadi Coalfields allotment if you applied, and keep an eye on US inflation data, oil near 91 dollars, and gold. Looking ahead, GDP numbers land on the thirtieth and the Reserve Bank's decision comes on the fourth of December. Have a good day.
